title: Forecast Evaluation & Cross-Validation
section: You have 5 forecasts. Which is best?
text:
You have 5 forecasts. Which is best?

Part A: How to score point forecasts fairly
Part B: Why 1 test split is not enough, and how rolling-origin CV fixes it








The deliverable is a reusable evaluation harness


A standard way to score any forecasting model, built and used today.




Pick this up from lecture 1 rather than restarting. They left the room with five forecasts and one number each, measured on a single 24-month window, and the STL route on top at 0.70. This lecture asks whether that number means anything.
The answer, twice over, is no: not with that metric, and not on that many windows.
Say what leaves the room today. By the end of Exercise 2.5 there is a file, labs/leaderboard.csv, with one row per benchmark and four columns that matter: MASE, RMSSE, scaled CRPS, and 80% coverage. Day 3 appends to that same file.
That framing is worth repeating at the end of every exercise in this lecture. The point of the harness is that adding a model to it is a few lines.

title: Forecast Evaluation & Cross-Validation
section: Only a scaled metric can compare across series
text:
Only a scaled metric can compare across series
Forecast error: \(e_{T+h} = y_{T+h} - \hat{y}_{T+h|T}\)








Metric
Property
Limitation




MAE
Easy to interpret
Scale-dependent: cannot be pooled across series


RMSE
Punishes large errors
Scale-dependent


MAPE
Unit-free
Explodes near zero, and asymmetric


MASE
Scaled: MAE over the benchmark’s
Needs the seasonal period


RMSSE
Scaled: RMSE over the benchmark’s
Same, and still punishes outliers




MAE and RMSE work well within a single series. To compare across different products or series, use MASE.

title: Forecast Evaluation & Cross-Validation
section: Rescaling the data moves MAE but not MASE
text:
Rescaling the data moves MAE but not MASE
Same series, new unit, with \(k > 0\): \(y'_t = k\,y_t\) and \(\hat{y}'_t = k\,\hat{y}_t\).

\[\text{MAE}' = \frac{1}{n}\sum \lvert k y_t - k\hat{y}_t \rvert = k\,\text{MAE}
\quad\text{(moves with the unit)}\]


\[PE'_t = \frac{k y_t - k\hat{y}_t}{k y_t} = PE_t
\qquad
\text{MASE}' = \frac{k\,\text{MAE}}{k\,Q} = \text{MASE}\]
Now shift as well as scale, \(y'_t = k y_t + c\), which is what °C to °F is. Differences kill \(c\), so MASE holds. MAPE’s denominator keeps it.

MAPE cancelled \(k\) and is still the worst metric in this deck. Cancelling is necessary, not sufficient.


Do this one at the board pace, not the slide pace. Ask what happens to each metric if the finance team reports the same series in thousands instead of dollars. Everyone knows MAE has to move. Then substitute.
MAE picks up the k and moves with the unit. MAPE cancels it, top and bottom. MASE cancels it too, and the reason is worth saying out loud: Q is built from the same data, so the denominator scales by exactly the same k as the numerator. That cancellation is the licence for what Day 1 did when it pooled 148 retail series with different turnovers into one ranking.
Then the sting. MAPE passed the test and is still the worst metric in this deck, so cancelling k is necessary and not sufficient. Add an offset and the two part company: every term in MASE is a difference, so c disappears, but MAPE divides by a level and the c rides along. That is the temperature objection, three slides early, and now it is a consequence rather than an assertion.

section: MAPE explodes when the actual is near zero
text:
MAPE explodes when the actual is near zero

PlotCode













# Dataset: simulated low-volume / intermittent demand (Poisson counts near zero)
low = D.low_volume_demand(n=48, seed=3)
preds = low[["ds"]].assign(A=low["y"] + 2.0,      # always 2 units too high
                           B=low["y"] - 0.15)     # always 0.15 too low

P.forecast_overlay(low, preds, ["A", "B"], history_tail=None,
                   history_label="actual (low volume)")




Forecast A: MAE = 2.00, MAPE = 304%
Forecast B: MAE = 0.15, MAPE = 23%


Read the two forecasts off the chart before quoting the numbers, and let the room commit. Forecast A is two units too high everywhere; forecast B is fifteen hundredths too low everywhere. Everyone picks B, and everyone is right.
Then show the MAPE column: A scores 304%, B scores 23%. MAPE agrees here. Now ask what happens when the actual is 0.2 and you are two units out - the percentage error is a thousand percent, and it is the denominator doing that, not the forecast.

title: Forecast Evaluation & Cross-Validation
section: Three reasons MAPE cannot select a model
text:
Three reasons MAPE cannot select a model

Undefined at zero: explodes on intermittent / low-volume demand
Asymmetric: penalizes over-forecasting far more than under-forecasting
Fails without a true zero: the offset never cancels, so °C breaks it


The second one surprises people, so make it concrete. Forecast 100 when the actual is 50 and MAPE charges you 100%. Forecast 50 when the actual is 100 and it charges you 50%. The same 50-unit error, twice the penalty for being high. A team that selects on MAPE learns to under-forecast, and in an inventory setting that means stocking out.
The third is the one people argue with, and the rescaling slide already answered it. MAPE needs a meaningful zero to divide by, and 0 degrees Celsius is not “no temperature”, it is a point on a scale somebody chose. Convert to Fahrenheit and the offset survives in the denominator, so the same forecast scores differently in the two units. MASE, built from differences, does not care.
None of this makes MAPE useless. It reports well to a business audience. It just cannot be the thing you select a model on.



Report MAPE to executives if required, but never optimize models using MAPE.

title: Forecast Evaluation & Cross-Validation
section: Dividing by the benchmark makes errors comparable
text:
Dividing by the benchmark makes errors comparable
Error divided by the in-sample Seasonal Naive error (\(Q\)):
\[\text{MASE} = \frac{\text{MAE}}{Q},
\qquad Q = \frac{1}{T-m}\sum_{t=m+1}^{T} \lvert y_t - y_{t-m} \rvert\]
\(Q\) is measured in the units of the data, which is what cancelled the \(k\).


\(\text{MASE} < 1\) \(\rightarrow\) Better than the seasonal naive baseline
\(\text{MASE} = 1\) \(\rightarrow\) Exactly as good as seasonal naive
\(\text{MASE} > 1\) \(\rightarrow\) Worse than simple baseline


The denominator is the whole idea: divide by the in-sample one-step seasonal naive error, and the metric becomes scale-free and readable. MASE below 1 beats the benchmark, above 1 loses to it.
Warn them the seasonal naive will score above 1 on this data, and that this is not a contradiction: forecasting 24 months out is harder than the one-step in-sample errors sitting in the denominator.

section: On this one window the STL route wins every metric
text:
On this one window the STL route wins every metric


                   MAE    RMSE  MAPE %   MASE  RMSSE
Mean            173.67  175.55   51.82  12.66   9.09
Naive            37.07   42.46   11.64   2.70   2.20
Seasonal naive   15.24   17.56    4.55   1.11   0.91
Drift            44.35   49.02   13.86   3.23   2.54
STL + drift       9.62   12.30    3.01   0.70   0.64



On this window the STL route wins on every metric (\(\text{MASE} = 0.70\)), with the seasonal naive second at \(1.11\). Hold that thought until part B.


Resist declaring a winner here. The seasonal naive’s MASE > 1.0 because forecasting 24 months ahead is harder than the in-sample one-step naive errors in the denominator. The STL route’s 0.70 is the number that gets a model promoted on one lucky year, and part B of this deck takes it back.
RMSSE is the same idea as MASE with squared errors, which is why the two columns agree on the ranking here and why both end up on the leaderboard.

title: Forecast Evaluation & Cross-Validation
section: One split gives a number with no error bar
text:
One split gives a number with no error bar

A single 24-month split is just one sample point
Score depends heavily on economic conditions during that window
High variance (\(\pm 16\%\) error bars on 24 observations)
Encourages data snooping and overfitting



Time series cannot use standard k-fold. We need rolling origins.


This is the hinge of the day. One split gives one number, and one number has no error bar, so it cannot support a ranking.
Ask the room how confident they would be in a drug trial with one patient. Same objection, same fix: more origins.

title: Forecast Evaluation & Cross-Validation
section: Rolling the origin turns one score into a distribution
text:
Rolling the origin turns one score into a distribution

PlotCode













# Diagram: the eight folds this deck scores on, drawn to scale.
# 144 periods, initial train 48, horizon 12, step 12 -> 8 origins.
P.cv_staircase(n_obs=144, initial=48, horizon=12, step=12)




Each fold trains only on past data. No fold ever peeks into its future.


Walk the diagram fold by fold. Blue is what the model saw, orange is what it was scored on, grey is the future it was not allowed to know about. Every row moves the boundary forward and never backwards.
Say explicitly why k-fold is wrong here: shuffling puts future rows in the training set, which is leakage, and the last slide of this deck comes back to it.

title: Forecast Evaluation & Cross-Validation
section: Three knobs control the CV: h, step_size, n_windows
text:
Three knobs control the CV: h, step_size, n_windows
# Rolling-origin CV on the spine:
cv = sf.cross_validation(
    df=spine,
    h=12,          # Forecast horizon matched to business need
    step_size=12,  # Steps between successive origins
    n_windows=8,   # Number of evaluation folds
    level=[80],
)

h: match the true operational planning horizon
step_size: frequency of forecast production
n_windows: number of independent test origins


Pick h from the decision, not from the data. If the plan is quarterly, h is three, and a model that wins at h=12 is not the one you want.
The trade in n_windows is honest: more windows is a steadier estimate and a shorter first training set. Eight is what this series affords.

The mean model scores exactly 0%. Not “poorly” - zero. On a series that grew sixfold, an interval centred on the historical average never touches the last few years at all, and that is worth pausing on: a model can be so wrong that its uncertainty estimate is not even wrong in an interesting way.
The seasonal naive’s 77% against a nominal 80% is the honest result here, and 96% on the single window in lecture 1 is the same interval measured badly.

title: Forecast Evaluation & Cross-Validation
section: Coverage checks the band. It cannot rank.
text:
Coverage checks the band. It cannot rank.
Ch 5.9 · Scoring the whole distribution

Coverage answers one question: is the 80% band honest?
It says nothing about width: an interval of \(\pm\infty\) covers 100%
Two models at 80% coverage can be worlds apart in usefulness
A proper score charges you for width and for misses, in one number



To score a distribution, we start by scoring a single quantile.


The infinity example lands immediately: an interval of plus or minus infinity has 100% coverage and zero value. Coverage is a pass/fail check on honesty, not a ranking metric. To rank models, we need a score that prices both width and misses fairly.

title: Forecast Evaluation & Cross-Validation
section: Quantile loss generalizes MAE to any level
text:
Quantile loss generalizes MAE to any level
A quantile forecast can miss low (\(y > \hat{q}_\alpha\)) or miss high (\(y < \hat{q}_\alpha\)). At \(\alpha = 0.9\) the two must not cost the same.

PlotFormula













\[L_\alpha(\hat{q}, y) = \begin{cases}
\alpha \, (y - \hat{q}) & \text{if } y \ge \hat{q} \quad \text{(underestimated)} \\
(1 - \alpha) \, (\hat{q} - y) & \text{if } y < \hat{q} \quad \text{(overestimated)}
\end{cases}\]





At \(\alpha = 0.5\) both slopes are \(0.5\): MAE was quantile loss all along.


Ask the room first: if you forecast the 90th percentile, how often should the actual value come in below your forecast? Ninety percent of the time! So being higher than actual is not a failure, it is the job. The penalty must reflect that expected asymmetry.
Then notice the slopes on the chart: at alpha=0.5, both sides rise at rate 0.5. That is plain absolute error divided by 2. When you minimize MAE, you are finding the median forecast.
At alpha=0.9, the slope to the right is 0.9 and to the left is 0.1. Setting the expected derivative to zero gives P(Y <= q) = alpha.

title: Forecast Evaluation & Cross-Validation
section: Winkler score combines two quantiles into an interval
text:
Winkler score combines two quantiles into an interval
An \(80\%\) prediction interval \([\ell_{0.2}, u_{0.2}]\) is bounded by the \(10\%\) and \(90\%\) quantiles.
\[\text{Winkler}([\ell, u], y) = \frac{L_{0.1}(\ell, y) + L_{0.9}(u, y)}{0.1}\]

Expanding the pinball losses gives a simple, intuitive charge:
\[\text{Winkler} = \begin{cases}
(u - \ell) & \text{inside the band} \\
(u - \ell) + \frac{2}{\alpha} (\ell - y) & \text{missed low } (y < \ell) \\
(u - \ell) + \frac{2}{\alpha} (y - u) & \text{missed high } (y > u)
\end{cases}\]



Winkler prices the trade: narrow intervals win inside the band, but pay a heavy linear fine for every unit outside.


The Winkler score is not a new ad-hoc formula. It is literally the sum of the two bounding quantile losses divided by alpha. When the actual observation falls inside the band, the score is simply the interval width (u - l). If it falls outside, the penalty is proportional to the distance of the miss.

title: Forecast Evaluation & Cross-Validation
section: Scaled CRPS averages quantile loss across all levels
text:
Scaled CRPS averages quantile loss across all levels

Quantile loss: scores a single quantile \(\hat{q}_\alpha\)
Winkler score: scores an interval \([\ell_\alpha, u_\alpha]\) (a pair of quantiles)
CRPS: scores the whole distribution by averaging quantile loss over all \(\alpha \in (0, 1)\)


\[\text{CRPS} = \int_0^1 2 \, L_\alpha(\hat{q}_\alpha, y) \, d\alpha \quad \approx \quad \frac{1}{|\text{levels}|} \sum_{\alpha} 2 \, L_\alpha(\hat{q}_\alpha, y)\]



Scaled CRPS divides by the seasonal naive benchmark error, making it scale-free and sortable across the entire portfolio.


This completes the arc from point forecast to distribution: MAE -> Quantile Loss -> Winkler Score -> CRPS -> Scaled CRPS. Now the room understands why LEVELS in scoring.py has a ladder of five levels (20, 40, 60, 80, 95): it provides 10 quantiles to approximate this integral.

text:
Narrow is not the same as good

PlotCode













# Dataset: Victorian takeaway food turnover, 8 rolling origins x 12 months
from utilsforecast.losses import scaled_crps

QCOLS = ["lo-95", "lo-80", "lo-60", "lo-40", "lo-20",
         "hi-20", "hi-40", "hi-60", "hi-80", "hi-95"]
QUANTILES = np.array([0.025, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.40, 0.60, 0.70, 0.80, 0.90, 0.975])

crps = {m: scaled_crps(cv.drop(columns=["cutoff"]),
                       models={m: [f"{m}-{c}" for c in QCOLS]},
                       quantiles=QUANTILES)[m].iloc[0] for m in MODELS}




The STL route’s intervals are the narrowest here, and it still loses on CRPS. Narrowness that is not earned gets charged for.


This is the Ch 5.9 payoff, so give it the time. It is the slide that stops “my intervals are tighter” from being an argument.
The STL route has the narrower 80% band - about 40 units against the seasonal naive’s 49 - and it loses on CRPS, 0.034 to 0.031, because those narrow bands miss more often: 61% coverage against 77%. Tighter is only better if you were right, and CRPS is what prices that trade in one number.

title: Forecast Evaluation & Cross-Validation
section: Choosing per fold with the answer in hand buys 24%
text:
Choosing per fold with the answer in hand buys 24%

# one rule fixed in advance, against the best model in each fold
honest = per_window["SeasonalNaive"].mean()
oracle = per_window[MODELS].min(axis=1).mean()

print(f"seasonal naive, every fold  : MASE {honest:.2f}")
print(f"best model, chosen per fold : MASE {oracle:.2f}")
print(f"discount bought by peeking  : {1 - oracle / honest:.0%}")

seasonal naive, every fold  : MASE 1.18
best model, chosen per fold : MASE 0.90
discount bought by peeking  : 24%



No rule available before a fold produces the second number. It is the holdout leaking into the choice of model.


Run this one live. The seasonal naive wins four folds and the STL route wins the other four, and swapping between them fold by fold takes the average from 1.18 to 0.90 - a 24% improvement bought entirely by knowing the answer first.
Ask the room what rule they would have written in advance to make those swaps. There isn’t one. That is the whole definition of leakage: a number produced by a decision that could not have been made at forecast time.
This is also the honest version of what happened in lecture 1, where a single window crowned the STL route at 0.70.

title: Forecast Evaluation & Cross-Validation
section: Four ways an honest team still fools itself
text:
Four ways an honest team still fools itself

Regime changes: verify if old folds disagree with recent folds
Underpowered sample: evaluate over sufficient origins (\(>50\) points)
Overlapping folds: step_size < h reuses points, so intervals read too narrow
Data gaps: verify timestamp continuity across all origins


None of these require anyone to be careless. Every one of them has shipped from a competent team.
If you have a war story, this is where it goes. If not, the honest version is the one this course just walked through: a single window crowned the STL route at 0.70 and eight windows handed it back.

title: ACF, Decomposition & Features
section: Eyeballing cannot be tested, and does not scale
text:
Eyeballing cannot be tested, and does not scale

Pick up from where we stopped: just before the exercise, the subseries plot could not show the spine’s seasonality underneath a sixfold trend. That was not a bad plot, it is the limit of looking.

Describing patterns by eye has a wider problem:

Does not scale: impossible across hundreds of series
Subjective: different people see different patterns
No significance test: cannot tell signal from noise








The Solution


Replace guesswork with numerical diagnostics: ACF, STL decomposition, and feature summaries.

title: ACF, Decomposition & Features
section: ACF is correlation with your own past
text:
ACF is correlation with your own past
Quantifies linear correlation between \(y_t\) and its lag \(y_{t-k}\):
\[r_k = \frac{\sum_{t=k+1}^{T}(y_t - \bar{y})(y_{t-k} - \bar{y})}{\sum_{t=1}^{T}(y_t - \bar{y})^2}\]

\(r_k \in [-1, 1]\)
\(r_1\) \(\rightarrow\) correlation with previous month (inertia/trend)
\(r_{12}\) \(\rightarrow\) correlation with same month last year (seasonality)
Plot \(r_k\) against \(k\) and you have a correlogram, the ACF plot


If you have ever done a scatterplot of x against y, you have done this. The only new thing is that x and y are the same column, offset by k.

title: ACF, Decomposition & Features
section: A lag plot on a trending series only shows the trend
text:
A lag plot on a trending series only shows the trend

PlotCode













# Dataset: Victorian retail takeaway turnover (spine = D.spine())
# Detrended with a 12-month centred moving average:
detrended = spine["y"].to_numpy() - P.centred_ma(spine["y"], 12)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(10, 4))
P.lag_plot_grid(spine["y"], lags=(1, 6, 12), axes=axes[0])
P.lag_plot_grid(pd.Series(detrended).dropna(), lags=(1, 6, 12), axes=axes[1])
axes[0, 0].set_ylabel("raw turnover ($M)", size=10)
axes[1, 0].set_ylabel("trend removed ($M)", size=10)




Raw (top): every lag scores \(r \approx 0.98\), which is the trend talking
Trend removed (bottom): lag 12 jumps to \(0.73\), lag 6 turns negative


The trend is removed here with a 12-month moving average, which is segment 4. Do not teach it yet. The point is only that the raw lag plot cannot separate the two.

title: ACF, Decomposition & Features
section: Bounds separate real correlation from luck
text:
Bounds separate real correlation from luck
White noise: no autocorrelation at any lag, every value independent of every other. For such a series:
\[r_k \sim N\left(0,\ \tfrac{1}{T}\right)\]


95% of autocorrelations fall inside \(\pm 1.96/\sqrt{T}\)
A spike inside the bounds is indistinguishable from noise
With 36 lags, ~1–2 spikes outside the bounds can occur by chance

title: ACF, Decomposition & Features
section: Slow decay: the spine ACF is dominated by trend
text:
Slow decay: the spine ACF is dominated by trend

PlotCode













# Dataset: Victorian retail takeaway turnover (spine = D.spine())
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 3.6))
P.acf_plot(spine["y"], nlags=36, ax=ax, highlight_every=12, ylim=(-0.15, 1.05),
           title="Spine ACF, 36 lags (annual lags in orange)")




Every lag sits far outside the bounds and decays slowly, which is trend
The annual lags (orange) are not spikes here: the trend swamps them


Ask why lag 12 is not a spike here when the seasonal plot was so obvious. Answer: every lag is already near 0.9 because of trend, so seasonality has no room left to show. Removing the trend is what the next segment does.

Key application: When the unexplained variation is white noise, the model has captured all systematic structure.

section: A log transform flattens the growing swing
text:
A log transform flattens the growing swing

PlotCode













# Dataset: Victorian retail takeaway turnover (spine = D.spine())
# Log transform: a multiplicative series becomes additive on the log scale
yt = np.log(spine["y"].to_numpy())

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.8))
P.plot_series(spine, ax=axes[0], title="Original: expanding swing", ylabel="turnover ($M)")
P.plot_series(spine.assign(y=yt), ax=axes[1], color=P.ORANGE,
              ylabel="log turnover", title="Log scale: constant swing")




When the swing grows with the level, take a log transform before decomposing
On the log scale a multiplicative series is additive: the swing stops growing
Forecasting on it? Back-transforming returns the median, not the mean (Ch 5.6)


Deck 1 named the diagnosis: the swing grows with the level, so the series is multiplicative, and the fix is the log transform. This slide is that fix, applied: the annual swing is now a constant size, and the sixfold trend has become a near-straight climb. Everything after this slide in the segment runs on the log-transformed series.
Box-Cox is the generalised version: a family of transforms indexed by lambda, with the log at lambda = 0. For this series the optimal lambda is about 0.07, so the log is the honest choice. Do not teach Box-Cox today; it comes back on Day 3 with ETS, where a fitted lambda is part of the model.
The median-vs-mean point is the one they will trip over in production: if a regional total is the sum of 40 back-transformed store forecasts, that total is biased low unless you correct it.

title: ACF, Decomposition & Features
section: A centred moving average estimates the trend-cycle
text:
A centred moving average estimates the trend-cycle
\[\hat{T}_t = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=-k}^{k} y_{t+j} \qquad (m = 2k + 1)\]

PlotCode













# Dataset: Victorian retail takeaway turnover (spine = D.spine(), last 15 years / 180 obs)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 2.2))
P.trend_overlay_plot(
    spine, {"3-MA": P.centred_ma(spine["y"], 3),
            "12-month MA": P.centred_ma(spine["y"], 12)},
    ax=ax, tail=180, colors=[P.PINK, P.ORANGE], ylabel="turnover ($M)",
    title="Spine, last 15 years: the order $m$ decides what survives")




Set the window to one seasonal period: \(m = 3\) keeps the season, \(m = 12\) erases it.


The 3-MA still wobbles because three months is a quarter of a cycle, so it averages a high month with two lower ones and keeps the shape. Twelve covers every month once. Twelve is even and has no middle month, which is the wrinkle the next slide deals with, so do not use the name 2x12-MA yet.

title: ACF, Decomposition & Features
section: A whole-cycle window cancels the season
text:
A whole-cycle window cancels the season
Averaging \(m = 2k+1\) terms of \(y_t = T_t + S_t + R_t\), centred on \(t\):
\[\hat{T}_t = \underbrace{\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=-k}^{k} T_{t+j}}_{\text{trend}}
            + \underbrace{\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=-k}^{k} S_{t+j}}_{\text{season}}
            + \underbrace{\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=-k}^{k} R_{t+j}}_{\text{noise}}\]

Constraint \(\sum_{j=1}^m S_j = 0\): ensures pure swings around trend (any non-zero mean is unrecognizable trend)
Season \(= 0\), exactly: an \(m\)-window spans one whole cycle
Trend survives: a symmetric window is unbiased on a linear trend
Noise shrinks by \(1/m\), damped but never removed


The constraint sum(S_j) = 0 is essential: without it, decomposition is not unique. Any non-zero average in S is unrecognizable trend, so the seasonal component is defined only up to a constant and the split between trend and season is not. Because the window is exactly one cycle, the middle term sums to 0. Locally linear trend offsets cancel, leaving T_t plus damped noise.
For a multiplicative model the same idea multiplies instead: going through a full cycle, S1 x S2 x … x Sm = 1, so a geometric mean over the window removes the season.

title: ACF, Decomposition & Features
section: Seasonal terms always sum to zero over \(m\) steps
text:
Seasonal terms always sum to zero over \(m\) steps
Periodicity (\(S_{t+m} = S_t\)) means any \(m\) consecutive terms span the full cycle:
\[\{S_{t-k}, \dots, S_{t+k}\} = \{S_1, \dots, S_m\} \qquad (m = 2k + 1)\]

Averaging over window \(m\) cancels the season completely:
\[\bar{S}_t = \frac{1}{m}(S_{t-k} + \dots + S_{t+k}) = \frac{1}{m}(\underbrace{S_1 + S_2 + \dots + S_m}_{\text{sums to } 0}) = \frac{1}{m}(0) = \mathbf{0}\]

Because additive seasonality sums to zero across one cycle by construction, any window of length m captures each season exactly once and averages to 0, regardless of the starting month.

title: ACF, Decomposition & Features
section: An even \(m\) needs the 2×\(m\)-MA to stay centred
text:
An even \(m\) needs the 2×\(m\)-MA to stay centred
Twelve months have no middle month: their average sits at \(t + \tfrac{1}{2}\). Average two adjacent 12-MAs to land back on \(t\):
\[\hat{T}_t = \tfrac{1}{24}y_{t-6} + \tfrac{1}{12}\sum_{j=-5}^{5} y_{t+j}
              + \tfrac{1}{24}y_{t+6}\]

PlotCode













# 2x12 Centred Moving Average filter weights:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 1.7))
P.ma_weight_plot(12, ax=ax, title="13 weights, symmetric about $t$")




\(y_{t-6}\) and \(y_{t+6}\) are the same calendar month, so between them it still gets \(\tfrac{1}{12}\), like every other month. The season cancels exactly.


The two half weights land on the same calendar month, six months either side of t. Between them that month still gets a full 1/12, like every other month, so the season still cancels exactly. That is the only reason the 2x12 form exists.

title: ACF, Decomposition & Features
section: Classical decomposition is averages all the way down
text:
Classical decomposition is averages all the way down

\(\hat{T}_t\) is the 2×12-MA
Detrend: \(y_t - \hat{T}_t\)
\(\hat{S}\) averages the detrended values within each month, then centres them to sum to zero
\(\hat{R}_t = y_t - \hat{T}_t - \hat{S}_t\)



Every piece is a moving average or a group mean. No fitting, no parameters. That simplicity costs something.


No fitting, no parameters, nothing to tune. That is its appeal and also its ceiling, which the next slide shows.

title: ACF, Decomposition & Features
section: The MA trend stops six months short of the present
text:
The MA trend stops six months short of the present

PlotCode

P.trend_overlay_plot(

    ax=ax, tail=60, colors=[P.ORANGE], shade_gap="2×12-MA trend",
    ylabel="turnover ($M)", title="Spine, last 5 years")




The first and last \(m/2\) observations get no trend estimate
The missing one is exactly where you forecast from


The other cost of classical decomposition: monthly means impose one seasonal shape on all 37 years. STL, next, fixes both problems at once.

title: ACF, Decomposition & Features
section: STL (Seasonal-Trend using Loess) splits all three
text:
STL (Seasonal-Trend using Loess) splits all three

PlotCode

res = STL(yt, period=12, robust=True).fit()
dcmp = spine.assign(
    **{"transformed turnover": yt},
    trend=np.asarray(res.trend),
    seasonal=np.asarray(res.seasonal),
    remainder=np.asarray(res.resid),
)
fig, axes = P.decomposition_plot(
    dcmp, ["transformed turnover", "trend", "seasonal", "remainder"],
    "STL decomposition of the transformed spine")

title: ACF, Decomposition & Features
section: STL bends where classical decomposition cannot
text:
STL bends where classical decomposition cannot

Adaptive: seasonal pattern can evolve smoothly over time
Flexible trend: estimates non-linear trend curves
Outlier-resistant: unusual spikes do not distort the trend (robust=True)
Remainder: isolates pure unexplained variation


STL = Seasonal-Trend decomposition using Loess. Key parameters: period (must provide) and seasonal window.

title: ACF, Decomposition & Features
section: Adjusting reveals the level shifts the season was hiding
text:
Adjusting reveals the level shifts the season was hiding

PlotCode













# Dataset: Transformed spine turnover (dcmp = STL components of transformed spine)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.5, 4.0))
P.adjusted_plot(dcmp, dcmp["transformed turnover"],
                dcmp["transformed turnover"] - dcmp["seasonal"], ax=ax,

The step up in 2009 and the dip around 2000 are level shifts, not season. Both are much easier to see once the annual swing is gone.

title: ACF, Decomposition & Features
section: One row per series makes a portfolio tractable
text:
One row per series makes a portfolio tractable

In practice, you manage hundreds or thousands of series
Manual visual inspection is impossible
Solution: Compute summary features (1 row per series)








Definition


A feature is a numerical summary of a whole series (e.g. trend strength, seasonal strength, entropy).

title: ACF, Decomposition & Features
section: Two numbers summarise a whole series
text:
Two numbers summarise a whole series
Using STL component variances:
\[F_T = \max\left(0,\ 1 - \frac{\text{Var}(R_t)}{\text{Var}(T_t + R_t)}\right) \qquad F_S = \max\left(0,\ 1 - \frac{\text{Var}(R_t)}{\text{Var}(S_t + R_t)}\right)\]


Values fall in \([0, 1]\)
\(F_T \approx 0\) \(\rightarrow\) No trend | \(F_T \approx 1\) \(\rightarrow\) Strong trend
\(F_S \approx 0\) \(\rightarrow\) No seasonality | \(F_S \approx 1\) \(\rightarrow\) Strong seasonality


Both are one minus a variance ratio. If the remainder is nearly as variable as the trend plus remainder, the trend is adding nothing and F_T is near zero. If removing the component barely changes the variance, the component was not there.

title: ACF, Decomposition & Features
section: Only seasonal strength separates the portfolio
text:
Only seasonal strength separates the portfolio

PlotCode













# Dataset: 148 Australian retail monthly series (allr = D.retail_all())
def stl_features(g):
    y = np.log(np.clip(g["y"].to_numpy(), 1e-6, None))
    r = STL(y, period=12, robust=True).fit()
    R, T_, S = np.asarray(r.resid), np.asarray(r.trend), np.asarray(r.seasonal)
    vr = np.var(R)
    return pd.Series({
        "trend_strength": max(0.0, 1 - vr / np.var(T_ + R)),
        "seasonal_strength": max(0.0, 1 - vr / np.var(S + R)),
    })

allr = D.retail_all()
feat = allr.groupby("unique_id")[["y"]].apply(stl_features, include_groups=False).reset_index()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.5, 4.3))
P.feature_scatter(feat, ax=ax, marks=[(hi, P.ORANGE, "most seasonal"),
                                      (mine, P.BLACK, "the spine"),
                                      (lo, P.PINK, "least seasonal")],
                  title="148 Australian retail series, both axes on the full 0 to 1 scale")




Every one of the 148 scores above 0.89 on trend strength and 97% score above 0.96, so trend tells you nothing about which series is which. Seasonal strength runs from 0.26 to 0.98, and that is the axis worth acting on.

Triage: focus manual attention on unusual series
Model Routing: skip seasonal models if \(F_S \approx 0\)
Anomaly Detection: feature outliers often indicate data errors
Clustering: group similar series for global models








Golden Rule


When a point looks anomalous in feature space, always plot the raw series.

title: Getting Started & Time Series Patterns
section: Forecasts exist to change decisions
text:
Forecasts exist to change decisions

Inventory: how much stock to hold
Staffing: how many people to roster
Energy: when generation must ramp up
Finance: cash flow and budget targets



A forecast is only useful if it changes a decision.


The decision dictates the entire setup: the forecast horizon, the time frequency, and the error metric you care about.

title: Getting Started & Time Series Patterns
section: Three factors dictate predictability
text:
Three factors dictate predictability

Understanding: how well we understand the drivers
Data: how much historical data exists
Influence: whether the forecast changes the outcome



Point 3 is key: if a demand forecast causes price cuts or stockouts, it alters future demand (self-fulfilling or self-defeating forecasts).

title: Getting Started & Time Series Patterns
section: High data and clear drivers make series predictable
text:
High data and clear drivers make series predictable



Electricity Demand

Clear physical drivers (weather, calendar)
High volume of historical data
Forecast does not change demand
\(\rightarrow\) Highly predictable




Exchange Rates

Weakly understood drivers
Forecast moves the market
No stable recurring pattern
\(\rightarrow\) Hard to beat today’s price

title: Getting Started & Time Series Patterns
section: Pure time series models require no future drivers
text:
Pure time series models require no future drivers
Forecasting hourly electricity demand (ED), three ways to write the same job:

1. Explanatory — why is demand what it is? Every driver on the right needs its own forecast first.
\[\small \text{ED} = f(\text{temperature},\ \text{economy},\ \text{population},\ \text{time of day},\ \text{day of week},\ \text{error})\]


2. Time series — what happened next last time? Everything on the right is already recorded.
\[\small \text{ED}_{t+1} = f(\text{ED}_t,\ \text{ED}_{t-1},\ \text{ED}_{t-2},\ \text{ED}_{t-3},\ \ldots,\ \text{error})\]


3. Mixed — dynamic regression: past demand plus drivers, so the drivers’ forecast error rides along.
\[\small \text{ED}_{t+1} = f(\text{ED}_t,\ \text{temperature}_{t+1},\ \text{time of day},\ \text{day of week},\ \text{error})\]

Course focus: Days 1–2 stay on model 2. Day 3 goes further.

This is fpppy 1.4. The point is not that explanatory models are worse — it is that their right-hand side is unavailable at forecast time, so you end up forecasting the predictors too, and inherit that error.

title: Getting Started & Time Series Patterns
section: Past history avoids missing future predictors
text:
Past history avoids missing future predictors
Time series models only need to know: what happened next last time?

External drivers may not be available
Future driver values are often unknown (e.g. future gas prices)
The real system is often too complex to specify


Relying on past history is not laziness; it is often the most dependable, honest model choice in production.

title: Getting Started & Time Series Patterns
section: Trend, seasonality, and cycles are distinct patterns
text:
Trend, seasonality, and cycles are distinct patterns

Trend: Long-term increase or decrease
Seasonality: Repeating pattern at a fixed, known period (day, week, year)
Cycle: Rises and falls with no fixed period (business cycles)


Trend does not have to be linear. Cycles are usually longer than seasonality and vary in length.

title: Getting Started & Time Series Patterns
section: Seasonality has a fixed calendar period; cycles vary
text:
Seasonality has a fixed calendar period; cycles vary



Seasonality

Known, fixed period
Driven by the calendar / clock
Can be counted on reliably




Cycle

Variable, unknown period
Driven by economic / natural factors
Turning points are hard to predict










Common Mistake


Treating a cycle as seasonality causes models to predict peaks at the wrong time with false confidence.

title: Getting Started & Time Series Patterns
section: Time series split into trend, season, and remainder
text:
Time series split into trend, season, and remainder

Additive: \(y_t = S_t + T_t + R_t\)
Multiplicative: \(y_t = S_t \times T_t \times R_t\)





Component
Meaning




\(S_t\)
Seasonal component (repeating calendar pattern)


\(T_t\)
Trend-Cycle component (underlying direction)


\(R_t\)
Remainder (random noise / unexplained variation)



Decomposition cannot separate trend from cycle, so \(T_t\) carries both. That is why it is written trend-cycle.

section: Expanding swings require multiplicative models
text:

Constant swing \(\rightarrow\) Additive
Growing swing \(\rightarrow\) Multiplicative (fix with log transform)

section: The Golden Rule
text:
The Golden Rule

The order is the data.



Never shuffle time series data
Never use random train/test splits
Never use standard k-fold cross-validation


Random shuffling allows models to look into the future. Day 2 introduces rolling-origin evaluation.

Same values, shuffled: every pattern is gone

section: Verify timestamp continuity before fitting models
text:
Verify timestamp continuity before fitting models

gaps = spine["ds"].diff().dt.days
print("Inferred frequency :", pd.infer_freq(spine["ds"]))
print("Duplicate stamps   :", spine["ds"].duplicated().sum())

Duplicate stamps   : 0
Gaps > 1 month     : 0









Silent Gaps Break Models


A missing row shifts every seasonal lag that follows. Always check frequency before modelling.

section: The Day 2 plan
text:
The Day 2 plan
Day 1 found the spine’s signal is seasonality. Day 2 builds the floor a model must beat, and the way to prove a forecast is real.

Four baseline models, plus the decomposition route: the floor to beat
Residual diagnostics: has the model taken all the signal?
Prediction intervals: the Gaussian formula, and why it fails here
Two repairs: resample the errors, then stop assuming a distribution








A forecast without a range is half an answer


A point forecast without an interval is an incomplete guess.




Open by picking Day 1 back up rather than restarting. Yesterday ended with the feature sweep: across 148 retail series trend strength was above 0.96 almost everywhere, so trend told you nothing, and seasonal strength was the feature that separated one series from another. That is the finding this whole day is built on. If seasonality is the signal, then the model to beat is the one that does nothing but repeat last year’s season - and that is where we start.
Say out loud what the day produces: a leaderboard file with real numbers in it, which Day 3 has to beat. Nobody leaves with a model today. They leave with the scoreboard.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: Four benchmarks set the floor a model must clear
text:
Four benchmarks set the floor a model must clear

Mean: average of all historical observations
Naive: last observed value (\(\hat{y}_{T+h} = y_T\))
Seasonal Naive: same season from previous year (\(\hat{y}_{T+h} = y_{T+h-m}\))
Drift: last value plus average historical trend slope



Always fit these 4 first. On many series, Seasonal Naive is tough to beat.


Do not let these sound like toys. On a seasonal series a seasonal naive is a genuinely hard opponent, and by the end of today they will have watched it beat a decomposition model over eight folds.
Worth saying which is which in plain language: the mean forgets time entirely, the naive remembers only yesterday, the seasonal naive remembers this month last year, and the drift draws a straight line through the first and last points. Ask the room which one they expect to win here before you show them.

section: Only one benchmark has the shape of the data

Only one benchmark has the shape of the data

The orange seasonal naive is the only one with the shape of the data in it. Let the room see that before any number is quoted.

section: A benchmark is what turns a score into evidence
text:
A benchmark is what turns a score into evidence

Objective evidence: proves the complex model adds value
Sanity check: catches complex ML models losing to naive rules
Scale baseline: provides a standard denominator for errors (MASE)
Fast: takes just a few lines of code








The question to ask in every review


“What is the simple baseline, and by how much did we beat it?”




This is the slide to slow down on if the room is senior. The question in the callout is the one to take back to work: it costs nothing to ask, and it is the single most effective check on a forecasting claim.
The MASE point is worth a sentence now because the metric arrives in lecture 2: the benchmark is not only a rival, it is also the denominator that makes errors comparable across series.

section: Decomposition is also a forecasting method
text:
Decomposition is also a forecasting method
Ch 5.7 · You already built every step on Day 1

Series\(y_t\) STLsplits off the season Forecastdrift · seasonal naive Recombineone forecast


The forecast carries the growth from one part and the shape from the other:
\[\hat{y}_{T+h} = \hat{A}_{T+h} + \hat{S}_{T+h}\]



MSTL(season_length=12, trend_forecaster=RandomWalkWithDrift()) is that whole chain in one object.


Ch 5.7. Every step is something they built yesterday: STL, the seasonally adjusted series, the seasonal component. The only new idea is that the two pieces can be forecast separately and added back.
The course pins trend_forecaster to drift on purpose: the default is AutoETS, which is Day 3’s material, and we do not want a Day 3 model quietly winning a Day 2 comparison.

text:
How drift and seasonal naive combine inside STL

PlotCode

# 2. Forecast A_t with Drift:             y-hat_{T+h} = A_T + h * drift_slope
# 3. Forecast S_t with Seasonal Naive:    y-hat_{T+h} = S_{T+h-m}
# 4. Recombine:                           y-hat_{T+h} = A-hat_{T+h} + S-hat_{T+h}

    freq=D.FREQ, n_jobs=1,
)

Walk the three panels from top to bottom: 1. Top panel: Seasonally adjusted series A_t. Drift extends it with a growth line. 2. Middle panel: Seasonal component S_t. Seasonal naive repeats last year’s shape. 3. Bottom panel: Summing both yields the recombined MSTL forecast (sky blue).

Do not let this land as “STL wins”. It wins on THIS window. Lecture 2 scores it over eight rolling origins and the ordering flips. Flag that now, so the reversal reads as the lesson rather than as a contradiction.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: Residuals flatter, forecast errors do not
text:
Residuals flatter, forecast errors do not
Residual (\(e_t\)): Error on in-sample training data (one-step ahead)
\[e_t = y_t - \hat{y}_{t|t-1}\]







Two errors to keep straight



Residuals = In-sample training errors (flattering)
Forecast Errors = Out-of-sample holdout errors (honest)





This distinction causes more confusion later than anything else in the day, so make it concrete: a residual is what the model got wrong on data it had already seen; a forecast error is what it got wrong on data it had not. Residuals flatter, forecast errors do not.
Everything in segment B is residuals. Everything in lecture 2 is forecast errors. Say that now and it saves a question later.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: Two failures mean fix the model, two mean fix the band
text:
Two failures mean fix the model, two mean fix the band



Essential: fix the model

Uncorrelated (\(r_k \approx 0\))
\(\rightarrow\) signal still on the table
Zero mean (\(\bar{e} = 0\))
\(\rightarrow\) forecast runs high or low




Useful: fix the interval

Constant variance
\(\rightarrow\) one width for all eras
Normally distributed
\(\rightarrow\) \(1.28\) is the wrong step





A model can pass the left column and fail the right. The point forecast is fine; the band around it is not.


Say the split as an instruction rather than as a taxonomy. A left-column failure is a message about the model: go back and change it. A right-column failure leaves the point forecast alone and tells you the band around it is wrong.
Pause on the dot before the bottom card and ask the room which column they expect the seasonal naive to fail. The next slide answers it.
One honest caveat if someone asks: uncorrelated appears on both sides. It is essential for the model, and it is also one of the three assumptions behind the Gaussian interval, which segment C spells out.
Segments C, D and E are, in order, the three ways to stop relying on the right column.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: The best benchmark here fails three of the four
text:
The best benchmark here fails three of the four

PlotCode













# fv = train merged with StatsForecast fitted values (sf.forecast(..., fitted=True))
resid = fv["y"] - fv["SeasonalNaive"]
P.residual_diagnostics(resid, ds=fv["ds"])




Zero mean fails: mean residual \(+7.9\), so the forecast runs low
Constant variance fails: SD \(8.5\) in the first decade, \(26.2\) in the last
Uncorrelated fails: ACF spikes stay outside the bounds


Three panels, and the three bullets read straight off them.
The time plot sits above zero far more than below, which is the bias: a seasonal naive repeats last year on a series that grows about 6% a year, so it runs low every month. Mean residual +7.9 against a series in the hundreds.
The same panel fans out, so constant variance fails. The ACF spikes well outside the bounds, so uncorrelated fails.
The fourth property, normality, is not on this slide because it is segment C’s business. The histogram is already telling you the answer if you look at it.
Do not treat any of this as a failure of the seasonal naive. It is the honest state of the best benchmark on this series, and every interval method later in this deck is a response to one of these lines.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: Ljung-Box tests all the lags at once
text:
Ljung-Box tests all the lags at once
\[Q = T(T+2)\sum_{k=1}^{\ell}\frac{r_k^2}{T-k}\]

\(p < 0.05\): autocorrelation is real, so the model is not finished
\(p \ge 0.05\): residuals are indistinguishable from white noise


r = resid.dropna()
p = acorr_ljungbox(r, lags=[24], return_df=True)["lb_pvalue"].iloc[0]
print(f"{len(r)} residuals, lag 24:  p = {p:.1e}")

405 residuals, lag 24:  p = 8.6e-241



Rule of thumb: use lag l=10 for non-seasonal data, l=2m for seasonal data.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: A range is what a decision can act on
text:
A range is what a decision can act on



Point forecast
“Demand will be 340 units.”

Guaranteed to be wrong
Hides the operational risk




Interval forecast
“Demand: [300, 380], 80% of the time.”

Sizes the safety stock
States the risk out loud




Decisions like staffing buffers, warehouse capacity, and safety inventory depend directly on the interval width.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: The future is a range, not a point
text:
The future is a range, not a point
At forecast origin \(T\), \(Y_{T+h}\) is still unknown:
\[Y_{T+h}\mid \mathcal{I}_T\]

Forecast distribution: plausible future values, given what is known at \(T\)
Point forecast: one centre, usually a mean or median
80% interval: 10th to 90th percentile
95% interval: 2.5th to 97.5th percentile



The unknown future value, not the prediction, is represented by a distribution.


Start with what is uncertain. We produce one point forecast, but we do not believe the future must equal that point. Before it is observed, we represent the future as plausible outcomes conditional on what we know now.
The point forecast is one summary. An interval takes two quantiles. The rest of the deck asks how to construct them: impose a Gaussian shape, simulate futures from empirical errors, or calibrate a set from past forecast errors.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: Gaussian intervals impose a shape
text:
Gaussian intervals impose a shape
Estimate the residual spread:
\[\hat{\sigma} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{T - K - M}\sum_{t=1}^{T} e_t^2}\]
Then step out from the point forecast:
\[\hat{y}_{T+1|T} \pm c\,\hat{\sigma}\]

\(K\) = estimated parameters; \(M\) = missing residuals
\(c = 1.28\) for 80%; \(c = 1.96\) for 95%


Two things students trip on. The M term: a seasonal naive cannot produce a fitted value for its first twelve months, so twelve residuals are missing and the denominator has to know that. And c is a normal quantile - 1.28 and 1.96 are only right if the residuals are normal, which we just showed they are not.
Flag that now. The rest of the deck is the repair.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: How fast the range widens depends on the method
text:
How fast the range widens depends on the method







Benchmark
\(h\)-step forecast standard deviation




Mean
\(\hat{\sigma}_h = \hat{\sigma}\sqrt{1 + 1/T}\)


Naive
\(\hat{\sigma}_h = \hat{\sigma}\sqrt{h}\)


Seasonal naive
\(\hat{\sigma}_h = \hat{\sigma}\sqrt{k+1}\),   \(k = \lfloor (h-1)/m \rfloor\)


Drift
\(\hat{\sigma}_h = \hat{\sigma}\sqrt{h\left(1 + \dfrac{h}{T-1}\right)}\)










\(\sqrt{h}\) is the naive case, not a law


For a seasonal naive the width is a staircase: flat inside a year, one step up per complete year crossed. \(k\) counts those years.




All four formulas assume the residuals are uncorrelated. That assumption is already known to be false here - segment B just rejected it at p ~ 1e-240.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: The interval is the forecast, the line is its middle
text:
The interval is the forecast, the line is its middle

PlotCode













# Dataset: Victorian retail takeaway turnover (train, test = D.train_test(spine, h=24))
# as_fan() renames one model's columns to ds / mean / lo-L / hi-L.
fc = sf.forecast(df=train, h=H, level=[80, 95])

P.fan_chart(train, as_fan("SeasonalNaive"), levels=(80, 95), actual=test,
            history_tail=72)




Make the room read the dashed actual line against the bands rather than admiring the shading. Ask how many of the 24 points fall inside the 80% band. It looks excellent here, and lecture 2 shows that a single 24-point window cannot measure a coverage rate at all.
If you want one sentence for this slide: the interval is the forecast, and the line down the middle is just its most likely value.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: The Gaussian interval rests on three assumptions
text:
The Gaussian interval rests on three assumptions

Residuals are uncorrelated: otherwise \(\hat{\sigma}\) understates the spread
Residuals have constant variance: one \(\hat{\sigma}\) for the whole series
Residuals are normally distributed: otherwise \(c = 1.28\) is the wrong multiplier



On this series all three fail. The next two methods each buy one of them back.


Count them off on your fingers, because the next three segments buy them back one at a time and it helps if the room is counting with you. Bootstrap buys back normality. Conformal avoids specifying a distributional shape, but replaces those assumptions with exchangeability. Distribution-free never means assumption-free.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: Resample the errors you actually saw
text:
Resample the errors you actually saw
A one-step error is \(e_t = y_t - \hat{y}_{t|t-1}\). For the naive method \(\hat{y}_{t|t-1} = y_{t-1}\), so \(y_t = y_{t-1} + e_t\), and a future value can be simulated by drawing a past error:
\[y^*_{T+1} = y_T + e^*_{T+1}, \qquad
  y^*_{T+2} = y^*_{T+1} + e^*_{T+2}, \qquad \dots\]

For the seasonal naive the same recursion runs on the seasonal lag:
\[y^*_{T+i} = y^*_{T+i-m} + e^*_{T+i}\]

The star means “one possible future that could have occurred”, not the observed value. Run it 5000 times and you have 5000 possible futures.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: The assumption you just made
text:
The assumption you just made

The simple residual bootstrap assumes the residuals come from one common distribution \(\hat{F}\) whose distributional characteristics do not change over time: i.i.d. draws from the pool of past errors.


Bought: normality. The interval is now whatever shape the errors are, and need not be symmetric.
Still owed: independence, and identical distribution.
On this series the second one is false: the residual SD tripled.


Every interval method spends an assumption; the honest question is which one. The bootstrap trades normality for identical distribution, and on this series that trade is a bad one - the residual SD tripled, so 1980s errors are in the same draw pool as 2010s errors.
That is not a reason to avoid the bootstrap. It is a reason to know which knob you are turning, and the lab turns it: restricting the pool to recent residuals moves coverage from about 61% to about 87%.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: 5000 possible futures
text:
5000 possible futures

PlotCode













# Dataset: Victorian retail takeaway turnover, seasonal naive residuals
resid_sn = (fv["y"] - fv["SeasonalNaive"]).dropna()

boot_paths = P.bootstrap_paths(train["y"], resid_sn, h=24, season_length=12,
                               n_paths=5000, seed=7)     # -> (5000, 24)
P.sim_paths_plot(train, fc["ds"], boot_paths, n_show=8, actual=test)




The band is not the method. The paths are the method; the band is a percentile taken down each column.


This is the slide that fixes the most common misconception about the bootstrap. Students see the shaded band and assume the band is the method. It is not. The method is these paths; the band is a percentile taken down each column afterwards.
Trace one path with your finger from the origin out to 24 months, and say: this is one possible future, drawn by taking last year’s value and adding a real error we actually observed at some point in the past.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: Dropping normality buys a fifth off the 80% band
text:
Dropping normality buys a fifth off the 80% band

PlotCode













# boot_fan = P.paths_to_fan(fc["ds"], boot_paths, levels=(80, 95))
#   -> ds / mean / lo-80 / hi-80 / lo-95 / hi-95, from empirical percentiles
P.fan_chart(train, as_fan("SeasonalNaive"), levels=(80, 95), actual=test)
P.fan_chart(train, boot_fan, levels=(80, 95), actual=test)




Mean 80% width: 59.7 Gaussian vs 46.4 bootstrap, a fifth narrower
Mean 95% width: 91.3 vs 90.1, the gap has closed
Sharp peak, fat tails. That is what excess kurtosis of 5.7 buys you


Same model, same point forecast, same data. Only the assumption changed, and the 80% band got a fifth narrower.
Notice the 95% bands barely differ. That is the shape of the residuals showing up exactly where you would expect it: the sharp peak makes the central 80% tighter, and the fat tails put the 95% back where the normal had it.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: Name the error first: \(e_{t+h|t}\)
text:
Name the error first: \(e_{t+h|t}\)
\[e_{t+h|t} = y_{t+h} - \hat{y}_{t+h|t}\]







Symbol
Meaning




\(t\)
the time the forecast was made: the forecast origin


\(h\)
the forecast horizon


\(t+h\)
the future time being predicted


\(y_{t+h}\)
what actually happened


\(\hat{y}_{t+h\,\vert\,t}\)
the forecast made at time \(t\) for time \(t+h\)









Note


At \(h = 1\) these are exactly the residuals from part B. For \(h > 1\) they are a different, wider set of errors, and they must be collected, not fitted.




Notation discipline pays off here. e_{t+h|t} carries two indices for a reason: which point is being forecast, and which origin it was forecast from. A 12-step error made in 2010 and a 12-step error made in 2016 are two members of the same calibration set.
Residuals had one index because there was only ever one origin: yesterday.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: A worked example of \(e_{t+h|t}\)
text:
A worked example of \(e_{t+h|t}\)

Walk-throughPlot


You hold \(y_1, y_2, \dots, y_{10}\) and want a 3-step-ahead interval.

Stand at \(t = 5\). Pretend \(y_6 \dots y_{10}\) do not exist yet.
Forecast three steps out: \(\hat{y}_{8|5}\).
Now look up what really happened: \(y_8\).
Record \(e_{{8|5}} = y_8 - \hat{{y}}_{{8|5}}\), one 3-step-ahead error.

. . .
Slide the origin to \(t = 6, 7, \dots\) and repeat. What you collect is the calibration set for \(h = 3\).















Walk this by hand on the numbers. Stand at t=5, the naive forecast for t=8 is whatever y_5 was, then look up what actually happened at t=8 and subtract. That single number is one member of the calibration set.
Slide the origin forward and you get another. Conformal prediction is nothing more elaborate than collecting those and taking a quantile of their absolute values.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: Distribution-free is not assumption-free
text:
Distribution-free is not assumption-free

Coverage requires the calibration errors and the next error to be exchangeable.


Shuffle their order: none should look as if it came from a different regime.


Use an empirical quantile of the collected errors:
\[\hat{y}_{T+h|T} \pm Q_{1-\alpha}(|e_{t+h|t}|)\]

One quantile per horizon \(h\): widening with \(h\) is measured, not assumed
No \(\hat{\sigma}\), no \(c\), no parametric shape: hence distribution-free


This is the slide that earns the segment, so do not rush it.
I.i.d. says every error is an independent draw from one fixed distribution. Exchangeability asks whether the calibration errors and the next error remain comparable when their order is shuffled. It can permit dependence that i.i.d. forbids, but it does not excuse a changing regime. If recent errors are systematically larger than old errors, their order carries information and exchangeability fails too.
Then the payoff. Because the interval is an empirical quantile of errors the model actually made, there is no sigma-hat to estimate and no c to look up, and nothing assumes a parametric shape. This constructs a calibrated prediction interval; it does not necessarily estimate a complete forecast distribution. That is why it works on a model whose interval has no formula, which is most of what Day 3 covers.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: Where the calibration set comes from
text:
Where the calibration set comes from

PlotCode













# Roll the origin backwards; keep the error at the horizon you care about.
cs = sf.cross_validation(df=train, h=12, step_size=12, n_windows=4)
cs12 = (cs[cs["ds"] == cs["cutoff"] + pd.DateOffset(months=12)]
        .rename(columns={"SeasonalNaive": "yhat"})[["cutoff", "ds", "y", "yhat"]])
P.h_step_error_diagram(train.tail(84), cs12)




statsforecast does exactly this internally: n_windows rolling origins, the absolute error at each horizon, then the empirical quantile of those.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: Any model at all can be given a conformal interval
text:
Any model at all can be given a conformal interval
from statsforecast.utils import ConformalIntervals

sf_conf = StatsForecast(
    models=[SeasonalNaive(
        season_length=12,
        prediction_intervals=ConformalIntervals(n_windows=8, h=24),
    )],
    freq="MS",
)
fc_conf = sf_conf.forecast(df=train, h=24, level=[80, 95])

n_windows: how many rolling origins make up the calibration set
Needs at least \(2h + 1\) observations; more windows, steadier quantiles
With 8 windows only 16 scores sit behind each horizon, so the band is visibly jittery


This is the practical payoff of the whole segment and the thing a Day 3 author will need: any model that has no closed-form interval gets one from prediction_intervals=ConformalIntervals(…). Not every statsforecast model can produce intervals on its own; all of them can produce conformal ones.
The jitter warning is worth making concrete. With eight windows there are only sixteen scores behind each horizon, so the band wobbles. That is a small sample showing through, not a bug.

section: One point forecast, three different bands
text:
One point forecast, three different bands

PlotCode

# fc       - Gaussian, from sf.forecast(..., level=[80, 95])
# boot_fan - P.paths_to_fan(fc["ds"], boot_paths)

    "Gaussian": (fc["SeasonalNaive-lo-80"], fc["SeasonalNaive-hi-80"]),
    "Bootstrap": (boot_fan["lo-80"], boot_fan["hi-80"]),
    "Conformal": (fc_conf["SeasonalNaive-lo-80"], fc_conf["SeasonalNaive-hi-80"]),

   method mean 80% width coverage (24 pts)
 Gaussian           59.7               96%
Bootstrap           46.4               88%
Conformal           59.2               96%



One point forecast, three bands. Left panel says they are not the same object; right panel says how they differ in shape. Gaussian is the staircase, bootstrap is narrow, conformal is jittery.
The printed numbers are the trap, so read them out and then say plainly where they came from: 24 points. The next slide is the arithmetic on why that cannot separate three methods.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: Every interval method spends an assumption
text:
Every interval method spends an assumption








Method
Assumes
Gives




Gaussian
uncorrelated · constant variance · normal
closed form


Bootstrap
uncorrelated · i.i.d. from \(\hat{F}\)
any error shape


Conformal
exchangeable \(h\)-step errors
no parametric shape









Important


Pick by which assumption you can defend, not by the widths on the last slide.




The table is the takeaway. Each row is a trade, and the honest question when choosing is not “which is most accurate” but “which of these three assumptions am I willing to make about this series”.
If the room wants a default: conformal, because it assumes least, and because it is the one that generalises to models that have no formula. That is also why it is the one Day 3 will lean on. But say the qualification out loud: its interval is distribution-free, not assumption-free, and a changing error regime can break exchangeability.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: Why one test window is misleading
text:
Why one test window is misleading
On a single small test set (\(n = 24\)), coverage error is large:
\[\text{SE} = \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}} = \sqrt{\frac{0.8 \times 0.2}{24}} \approx \pm 8\% \quad (\pm 16\% \text{ at } 95\% \text{ CI})\]


A nominal 80% interval could easily measure anywhere from 64% to 96% on a single 24-point holdout by chance alone.



Over 8 rolling origins (96 scored points) they separate cleanly:


80% coverage over 96 scored points:   Gaussian 77%   bootstrap 61%   conformal 83%



The bootstrap’s 61% is the identically-distributed assumption being punished: pooling 1980s residuals (SD 8.5) with 2010s residuals (SD 26) makes the draw pool far too tight for a forecast issued in 2016. Restricting the pool to the last 120 residuals takes it to about 87%; the last 60 push it to 91%. The assumption is the knob, and the lab turns it.
